clue.text: Stadium's 12 tiers back housing appeal to Lord Coe

indicators.note: housing means holding something inside, so the row letters wrap around the appeal

parts.note: in a theatre the twelfth row back from the front is row L, the twelfth letter of the alphabet
Lord Coe is the athlete Sebastian Coe, known as Seb; an appeal to him is the vocative O SEB

explanation.surface: A stadium with a dozen tiers of seating calls on Lord Coe, the London 2012 Olympics chief.
explanation.walkthrough: '12 tiers back' is not a count of tiers: it is ROW L, the twelfth row. 'housing' puts O SEB inside it, after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rose Bowl is the famous football stadium in Pasadena, California, home of the annual college game.

clue.text: Woman's dress sets off fine diamond

indicators.note: sets off is read as sends away, so the letter for fine is dropped from the dress

parts.note: a frock is a woman's dress
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: A woman's outfit is shown at its best by a good diamond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sets off' looks like 'shows to advantage', but it means removing the F from FROCK.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock is slang for a gemstone, especially a diamond in an engagement ring.

clue.text: Like a cold seat on the gravy train?

definitions.text: Like a cold seat on the gravy train?

parts.words: Like a cold seat on the gravy train?
parts.note: a common cold has no remedy, it is 'without ...' (Latin ... cura), and a cushy post on the gravy train is one with no duties

explanation.surface: A chilly seat on a train carriage, of the kind politicians who feather their nests ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Sine is Latin and Chambers for 'without', so a cold is 'sine cure'; the whole answer is a paid job with no work, a seat on the gravy train.
explanation.definitionFit: A post that pays well for little or no work is the classic gravy-train seat.

clue.text: He's not troubled with tumult in a little margarine spread

definitions.text: He's not troubled with tumult in a little margarine spread

indicators.note: spread means scattered about, so the letters before it are laid out afresh

parts.words: He's not troubled with tumult in

indicators.note: a little of the margarine is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone serene amid chaos is compared to margarine so cool it never softens.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes every letter of 'He's not troubled with tumult in' plus M, the first of 'margarine', signalled by 'a little'; 'spread' is the anagram signal, while also suggesting the margarine.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone who looks utterly calm and innocent, untouched by any heat or fuss around them.

clue.text: See 3
Cage St!

definitions.meaning: to cage someone is to lock them in, confine them
St! is an old call for quiet, meaning be silent

explanation.surface: Two words that read like a shouted instruction about a cage.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both to confine something (as in a cage) and the order 'be quiet!', which 'St!' expresses.

clue.text: See 3
Work of weather people, half looking up in anticipation of trouble

indicators.note: in anticipation of puts the first piece ahead of the second
in a down clue looking up means read upwards, so the latter half of the weather service is turned round

parts.note: the Met is the Meteorological Office, Britain's weather service
a pest is a nuisance or trouble

explanation.surface: Weather forecasters, half of them peering skyward, await a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half looking up' turns only the MET of THE MET, giving THE TEM. The Met Office is Britain's national weather forecaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's late play is a work, fittingly opening with a storm, which the forecasters' trouble hints at.

clue.text: Tube to Barking? Show children the way to go

definitions.meaning: read as a London Underground train to Barking, a station in east London, made silly: a train that is barmy

definitions.text: Show children the way to go
definitions.meaning: teach toddlers to use a chamber pot instead of nappies

explanation.surface: Directions for children on the Underground to Barking.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is an east London district on the Tube; 'barking' is also British slang for mad, so a barking train is a crazy one.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet training is literally teaching children where to go when they need to go.

clue.text: Interpreted reductions suspiciously (getting one free)

indicators.note: suspiciously suggests something fishy has been done to the letters, so they are rearranged
one is the Roman numeral I, and getting it free means letting it go from the word

explanation.surface: Price cuts were viewed with suspicion when a free item came with them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting one free' drops the I from REDUCTIONS; 'suspiciously' rearranges the remaining nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To construe a remark is to interpret its meaning, so the past tense matches interpreted.

clue.text: Come to an unexpected end, as addition to private bill going through Parliament?

indicators.note: going through means passing inside, so the addition sits within the assembly

parts.note: a diet is a legislative assembly, as in the Japanese Diet
something added to your own charge is on one's fee

explanation.surface: A private bill passing through Parliament meets an unexpected end, with a charge tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private bill' looks like legislation, but here it is someone's own invoice, with something added on top. A diet is a parliament in several countries, such as Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: To die still standing, while still active, is to come to an end nobody saw coming.

clue.text: Something for the bed made from these?

indicators.note: made from says the item is fashioned out of the letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what bedding could be made out of these materials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made from' is the anagram signal: rearrange THESE.
explanation.definitionFit: A linen sheet is a piece of bedding laid over the mattress.

clue.text: Gong sounded by wretched Moyles so intrusive

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase, in such an intrusive way, matching the adverb

indicators.note: this word only joins the neighbouring pieces: it says which one stands next to which in the answer
sounded means spoken, so a word with the same sound as the decoration is meant

parts.note: gong is British slang for a medal or decoration

indicators.note: wretched means in a sorry state, so the radio presenter's name is jumbled

explanation.surface: Chris Moyles, the brash British radio DJ, gets an award and is barged in on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounded' gives MEDDLE from MEDAL (gong); 'wretched' rearranges MOYLES to SOMELY. Chris Moyles is a British breakfast-radio DJ. 'so intrusive' is read as an adverb phrase, 'in so intrusive a way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting meddlesomely means poking into others' affairs, the manner of an intrusive busybody.

clue.text: "End of the line" letter on valentine's card to Mrs Simpson?

definitions.meaning: a London railway terminus, where trains finish their journey

definitions.text: letter on valentine's card to Mrs Simpson?
definitions.meaning: a kiss is written as the letter X, a cross; one sent to Wallis Simpson would come from Edward VIII, a king

explanation.surface: A note on a love card, signed off to Wallis Simpson.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward VIII gave up the throne in 1936 to marry the American divorcee Wallis Simpson, so his X on her valentine is a king's cross.
explanation.definitionFit: King's Cross is a major London mainline terminus, literally where lines end; the X kiss from a monarch is the pun.

clue.text: 0 or 1, then 10 — or, on the face of it, 3,4,6, then 7?

definitions.meaning: on the Beaufort wind scale force 0 or 1 is still air, and force 10 is a gale of the most violent kind, so quiet comes first and fury follows

definitions.text: on the face of it, 3,4,6, then 7
definitions.meaning: a face looking unruffled, as in the long phrase across 3, 4 and 6, followed by Shakespeare's tempest play at 7, sketches peace preceding upheaval

explanation.surface: A string of numbers and cross-references, like a code to decipher.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beaufort scale grades wind from 0 to 12; 'or' joins two readings. The second uses grid answers: a placid face, then The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names an eerie quiet that precedes trouble, like still air ahead of a gale or a serene face ahead of a tempest.

clue.text: A twist of celery as inherent goodness!

indicators.note: a twist turns the extracted letters the other way round
of says the letters are taken from within the clue words that follow

explanation.surface: A cocktail with a twist of celery, praised for its natural virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' picks YASI out of 'celerY AS Inherent'; 'A twist' turns it round. 'goodness!' is the exclamation, not the moral sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild British exclamations of surprise, interchangeable as 'Well, goodness!'

clue.text: Shorthand recorder sent poetry for review

indicators.note: for review suggests going over the material again, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A secretary taking dictation who has sent off poems to be reviewed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for review' rearranges SENT POETRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A stenotyper operates a stenotype machine to take down speech in shorthand.

clue.text: See 14
Pinkerton's work setting for choppers, scrapers in hand

parts.note: choppers is slang for teeth, which are set in the gums
with hoes in your hands you are hoeing, scraping at weeds

explanation.surface: A dentist's job of fitting false teeth, with tools in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinkerton's was the famous American detective agency, so 'Pinkerton's work' is detecting; the surface leans toward dentistry.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumshoe is a private detective, so gumshoeing is detective work, the business of a Pinkerton agent.

clue.text: Italian wine's up 80%

indicators.note: eighty per cent of a five-letter word is its opening four letters, so the end is lost

parts.note: out of bed, stirring

explanation.surface: The price of an Italian wine has gone up by eighty per cent.
explanation.walkthrough: '80%' keeps four of ASTIR's five letters, dropping the R.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling white from Piedmont, named after its home town.

clue.text: Either side of Channel I voiced disapproval aboard water vehicle

indicators.note: aboard means on board, so the disapproving sound is carried inside

parts.note: the word for I in French (JE) and in English (I), from either side of the English Channel
tsk is the clicking sound of disapproval

explanation.surface: Someone tutting while riding a jet ski across the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel is the English Channel: France on one side, England on the other, so 'I' is given in both languages, one at each end of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A jet ski is a small motorised personal watercraft ridden like a motorbike.

clue.text: Bare pass (Group A) obtained in old Roman city sampler

indicators.note: obtained in says the grade and group end up inside the city

parts.note: Chester was the Roman city of Deva in north-west England
E is the lowest pass grade, one above a fail
a set is a group, followed by A as written

explanation.surface: A student scrapes a pass in Group A at a school in an old Roman city.
explanation.walkthrough: In British exam grading E is the lowest pass, just above a fail. Chester, in north-west England, was the Roman fortress of Deva.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who samples cheese for quality, a grader or taster, is a sampler.

clue.text: See 2
Block series of TGVs to Paris

indicators.note: series of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Barricading a line of high-speed French trains heading for Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: TGVs are French high-speed trains; the hidden letters straddle 'TGVs to Paris'.
explanation.definitionFit: To block something is to halt it, prevent its progress.

clue.text: Totally silent, it appears, over architectural feature

parts.note: with no sound at all, at zero volume, written O VOL
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: An ornate building feature that seems to make no noise at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Zero (O) volume (VOL) is total silence; 'it appears' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovolo is a convex quarter-round moulding used in classical buildings.

clue.text: Adolescent problems? Daughter accepted reverses couldn't be helped

indicators.note: reverses means turned back, so everything built so far is read backwards
accepted means taken in, so the youngster holds the other pieces

parts.note: a teen is an adolescent
sums are maths problems

explanation.surface: A teenager's troubles: a daughter took setbacks that couldn't be avoided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adolescent problems?' reads as one idea but splits into two pieces, the youngster and the sums; 'reverses' looks like setbacks but turns the whole build round.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'needs must when the devil drives' says something had to happen; it is said of things unavoidable.

clue.text: Tropical divers mistakenly missing broken link

indicators.note: divers is the old adjective for various, so the letters are put in different order

explanation.surface: Scuba divers in the tropics made a mistake and lost a broken link from their chain.
explanation.walkthrough: MISTAKENLY with the letters of LINK removed ('missing broken link') leaves MSTAEY, which 'divers' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropical weather is hot and humid, and humid heat is described as steamy.

clue.text: Protest's afoot: start singing!

parts.note: a strike is a protest by withholding labour
afoot means happening, going on, which is up, as in 'what's up?'

explanation.surface: A rallying cry on the picket line: the protest is on, so sing!
explanation.definitionFit: To strike up a tune is to begin playing or singing it.
